label: Parenting Struggles
framing: No one parents from a position of mastery. Scripture hands the work to ordinary parents, tells them to teach as they walk and sit and lie down, and never pretends it will be clean or finished by Friday.
cultural: In the world of the Hebrew Scriptures the household was the school, the trade, and the sanctuary all at once, and raising a child was the slow daily handing on of a whole way of life. The command to teach diligently was given to parents who farmed and traded and worried, not to experts, and it assumed the lessons would be passed in the dust of the road, not in a special hour set apart.
historical: The early church startled Rome by refusing to abandon unwanted infants and by treating children as full members of the covenant. Augustine in the fourth century wrote with painful honesty about his own childhood and his mother Monica's long patience, John Chrysostom preached that raising a child well was a parent's highest art, and the Reformers placed the family, not the school, at the center of a child's formation in faith.
application: Aim for faithfulness over performance, since the parent who is present and repentant teaches more than the parent who is perfect. Discipline to shape, never to vent, and let your children see you apologize when you get it wrong. Hand on the faith in the ordinary hours rather than saving it for a lecture. And carry the weight you cannot fix to God, who loves them more than you do and is not finished with them.

verses.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat— for He gives sleep to His beloved.
verses.where: A song of ascents, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. In Hebrew a house meant a household as well as a building, so the builders here include parents. Rising early and staying up late cannot do what only the LORD does, and he gives sleep to those he loves.

verses.text: These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts. And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
verses.where: Moses gives Israel the heart of the law: the LORD is one, and he is to be loved with everything. The words are to be on the parents' own hearts first. Only then are they taught, and they are taught in ordinary places: at home, on the road, at bedtime and at breakfast.

verses.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verses.where: In a Roman household the father held legal power over his children as long as he lived, and harsh discipline was common. Paul tells children to obey, and then puts a limit on the father that ordinary household rules did not: do not provoke your children to anger.

verses.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged.
verses.where: Ancient writers on the household spoke to the head of the house about managing his dependents. Paul speaks to children directly, as people responsible to the Lord, and gives fathers a duty with a reason: a child who is constantly provoked loses heart.

verses.text: Because Isaac had a taste for wild game, he loved Esau; but Rebekah loved Jacob.
verses.where: Isaac loves Esau and Rebekah loves Jacob. The Bible sets down the favoritism without comment, and the next chapters show what grows from it: a deception, a stolen blessing, and a brother who wants to kill his brother.

verses.text: When His parents saw Him, they were astonished. “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.”
verses.where: Mary and Joseph are a full day's travel home from Passover before they notice that the twelve-year-old Jesus is not with them, and they search three days. Mary's words are a rebuke full of fear. Even the parents of Jesus did not understand him at once, and Luke says he went home with them and grew.

verses.text: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”
verses.where: Jesus is teaching his disciples to pray. He points to something every parent in the crowd knew: no father hands a hungry son a snake instead of a fish. Parents who are themselves sinful still know how to give good things, and the Father in heaven gives more.

verses.text: He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He gently leads the nursing ewes.
verses.where: Isaiah announces that God is coming to his exiled people as a mighty king. In the same breath he describes him as a shepherd who carries the lambs and gently leads the ewes that are nursing their young. The strength of God and his gentleness with the weary are one.

verses.text: For you know that we treated each of you as a father treats his own children— encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory.
verses.where: Paul reminds a young church how he cared for them, and he reaches for the pictures of a nursing mother and a father. The father's work, as he describes it, is encouraging, comforting and urging, with the goal of a life worthy of God.

verses.text: But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
verses.where: The disciples try to keep children away from Jesus, as if they were an interruption. Jesus is indignant, the only time the Gospels use that word of him, and he says the kingdom belongs to such as these. He takes them in his arms and blesses them.

links.label: Parenting is harder than anyone said

misread.taken: This verse, often remembered as “spare the rod, spoil the child” (a saying that is not in the Bible), has been used to justify punishment given in anger, and harm that leaves marks, as a parent's religious duty.
misread.says: The proverb's target is the parent who never corrects at all, which it calls a failure of love. It assumes a parent who loves the child and aims at the child's good, not a parent venting frustration. The word for rod also names a shepherd's staff and a ruler's scepter, and Proverbs uses it of correcting adult fools as well as sons. Faithful Christians differ on whether the verse speaks of physical discipline (see below), but no reading of it permits injury or abuse, which the whole Bible condemns, and it must be read beside the command not to provoke children (Ephesians 6:4).
misread.text: He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently.

misread.taken: The “quiver full” of verse 5 is used to rank families: the more children, the more blessed and faithful the parents, and the smaller or childless home falls short.
misread.says: The psalm calls children a heritage, a gift handed down, not a wage earned. In its world, grown sons were a household's protection, the people who stood beside their father when he faced opponents at the city gate where disputes were settled. The psalm praises children as God's gift; it does not measure anyone's faith by their number, and Scripture honors those who have no children, among them Jesus himself.
misread.text: Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward. Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are children born in one’s youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate.

whole: Parenting struggles come in every size. A toddler who will not sleep, a ten-year-old who lies, a teenager who has gone silent, a child with needs nobody prepared you for, or simply the exhaustion of doing it day after day with too little help. Underneath most of them sits the same fear: that you are getting it wrong, and that your child will pay for it. Christian parents often add a second weight, the sense that a godly home should look calmer than theirs does.

The Bible is more honest about families than most parenting advice. Its homes are full of trouble: Isaac and Rebekah each with a favorite, Eli unable to restrain his sons, David's household torn apart, and Mary and Joseph searching three days for a son they did not understand. Scripture does not present a model family to copy. It presents a God who keeps working through families that are not models, and who calls himself a Father who gives good gifts even to children who have not earned them.

What the Bible asks of parents is smaller and harder than a method. The words are to be on your own heart first; children learn faith mostly from what they watch, at the table and on the road, before they learn it from what they are told. Discipline is real and necessary, and Proverbs has no patience for the parent who never corrects. But the New Testament adds, twice, the command that parents in Paul's world did not expect to hear: do not provoke your children, or they will lose heart. Correction that comes from a parent's anger or pride teaches a child something other than wisdom.

That leaves room for grace in both directions. Parents will fail, sometimes in ways their children remember for years, and the path forward is the ordinary one of the Christian life: confess it, ask forgiveness, including from the child, and keep going. The psalm says that unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. That is not a reason to stop building. It is permission to sleep, and to remember that the child belongs to God before they belong to you.

differ.share: Christians agree that children are a gift from God and bearers of his image, that parents are called to teach and correct them in love, that no discipline may harm or abuse a child, and that a child's faith is finally God's work.

views.name: Measured physical discipline
views.body: Many Christians read Proverbs 13:24, with 22:15, 23:13-14 and 29:15, as endorsing measured physical discipline for young children, given calmly, privately and in love, never in anger, and always with the aim of the child's good. They note that the proverb's point is that withholding correction is a failure of love.

views.name: Discipline without the rod
views.body: Other Christians hold that the rod in Proverbs stands for correction in general, since the same book uses it of adult fools, and that Proverbs describes the methods of its own culture rather than a technique for every age. They discipline through consequences, instruction and close relationship, often citing the command not to provoke children (Ephesians 6:4, Colossians 3:21).

views.name: Children and baptism
views.body: Christians also differ on the place of children in the church. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize the infants of believers as members of the covenant community; Baptist and many other churches dedicate infants and baptize on a person's own profession of faith.

differ.after: All of them call parents to love, patience, instruction and correction without harm, and all of them pray for their children's faith as something only God can give.

deep.sit: What do your children see in you on an ordinary Tuesday that teaches them what you actually believe about God?

prayer.lead: A prayer of Moses that asks for God's work to be seen by the next generation, and for the work of tired hands to last.
prayer.text: May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children. May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands— yes, establish the work of our hands!
